sources: P4-F1 speed. Acosta, C. A. (2003), 'The House Centipede (Scutigera coleoptrata; Chilopoda): Controversy and Contradiction', J. Ky. Acad. Sci. 64(1):1-5, Dept. of Biological Sciences, Northern Kentucky University (scanned PDF on NKU's site; OCR slips fixed in the quote): "They have been clocked at 420 mm./sec with a 33 mm stride, which was impressive enough to be listed as among the fastest arthropods in the 1973 Guinness Book of World Records." (420 mm/s = about 16.5 inches a second); https://websites.nku.edu/~acostac/AcostaJKAS2000.PDF ; Mississippi State University Extension, Bug's Eye View, House Centipede (No. 29, 2015): "They are also able to run much faster than most other ground-dwelling arthropods, reaching speeds approaching one MPH."; https://www.accessibility.extension.msstate.edu/newsletters/bugs-eye-view/2015/house-centipede-no-29

P4-F2 run, stop, freeze; up walls. University of Arkansas Arthropod Museum, House centipede: "The house centipede is often seen darting across floors at high speed, occasionally stopping suddenly and remaining motionless for some time before racing off once more."; https://arthropod.uark.edu/house-centipede/ ; University of Kentucky Entomology, fact sheet ef645, Centipedes and Millipedes in and Around the Home (Gordon, Larson, DeVries): "To aid in hunting, house centipedes can run very quickly across floors and up walls."; https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef645

P4-F3 pounce and lasso. University of Arkansas Arthropod Museum, House centipede: "They capture prey by half pouncing and half lassoing them."; https://arthropod.uark.edu/house-centipede/ ; Acosta 2003 (above): "The long legs of S. coleoptrata function primarily for chasing and catching mobile prey."

P4-F4 eyes. University of Arkansas Arthropod Museum, House centipede: "Unlike most other centipedes, house centipedes and their close relatives have well-developed, faceted eyes."; https://arthropod.uark.edu/house-centipede/ ; Acosta 2003 (above): "House centipedes have large heads, prominent compound eyes, long annulated antennae, and very long legs." and "Behind the antennae is a pair of modified compound eyes, in contrast to other chilopods which have simple ocelli."

P4-F5 grooming. Acosta 2003 (above), citing Le Moli and Parmigiani 1976 and Verhoeff 1938: "House centipedes meticulously groom themselves on a strict schedule (Le Moli and Parmigiani 1976). The antennae and legs are gripped by the forcipules and passed through the cleaning setae on the first maxillae (Verhoeff 1938b)."; "If an individual is interrupted for any reason during grooming, cleaning commences where the individual left off prior to being disturbed."; "Grooming behavior appears to be genetically hard-wired because house centipedes will still attempt to clean legs that have been amputated."; https://websites.nku.edu/~acostac/AcostaJKAS2000.PDF

P4-F6 breathing holes on the back. Acosta 2003 (above): "The seven tergites each bear a median dorsal spiracle for gas exchange, unlike the lateral paired spiracles of other myriapods." (tergites = the back plates; dorsal = on the back; median = down the middle); https://websites.nku.edu/~acostac/AcostaJKAS2000.PDF

P4-F7 eggs. Acosta 2003 (above), citing Lewis 1981: "Females lay relatively few eggs (average four eggs per day; Lewis 1981), singly in soil. Laying and hatching occurs from late spring through early summer."; University of Arkansas Arthropod Museum: "Eggs are laid in spring and early summer."; https://arthropod.uark.edu/house-centipede/
P4-F8 newly molted males. Acosta 2003 (above): "Newly molted male house centipedes are especially susceptible to predation by females."; https://websites.nku.edu/~acostac/AcostaJKAS2000.PDF
Mississippi State University Extension (via Social Studio QA channels/qa/centipede-p4-1117.md): "Bites to humans are uncommon unless centipedes are handled or accidentally pressed against the skin."

beats.say: Don't squish it! You just saw a bug Guinness listed among the fastest arthropods.
Squish it, or let it live? Vote at the end.
Clocked at about sixteen inches a second. Close to one mile an hour.
Will it bite you? Bites are uncommon, and usually only if you handle it or press it against your skin.

beats.say: It darts, sometimes stops dead, and can freeze for a while.
It catches its food by half pouncing, half lassoing.
It can run up your walls to hunt. Meatball checked his walls. Hell, no!
Unlike most centipedes, it has well-developed, faceted eyes. Meatball's eyes need coffee.
But the weirdest part? How it cleans itself.
On a strict schedule, it pulls each leg through its mouthparts. Like floss.
It even tries to clean legs it doesn't have anymore. Damn. Meatball skips the legs he has.
It breathes through holes down the middle of its back. Meatball breathes through his mouth.
Moms lay eggs one at a time, in soil. His dog, Noodle, heard soil and started digging.
A male that just molted is especially vulnerable to being eaten by a female. Meatball cancelled his date.
So, does the speedy roommate stay, or get squished?
